text:
Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

The Laste Daye II

The next storme came upone a nyght without sterres. The zee struck from two quarters at once; abouve, the sayle bræst loose and floggede the mast like a furieux flagellante. Beneath, the oores took such weyghte that every banke strained to lyfte them from the watere.

Vettore cried commaunds from the decke. Niko came down to the benches with a stycke, though feare made his strokes fall wide. Matteo had eaten no more than a thumb of byscuite in two dayes. He held the shafte opposite Cane, his face pallid in the swyngynge lanterne. On oon false pulle he roose too soone. The greate oore cæm backe agaynst him.

He dropped. Cane saw it across the passauge. The banke behind him was already leanynge into the next stroke. To loose his holde would drive the shaft among six men's faces; to reach the boy he must cross two chained rowes and the running oore. He shouted instead.

“Matteo!”

The boy stirred beneathe the bench, coughed, and brought blode to his lips. Nico ordered him upright. He could not rise. Nico hit him, once, and the Greke called out that his blowes would not mend a broken rib nor empty a drowned lung.

“Then make him pull!” Nico shouted.

Vettor's voice came through the hatch.
“TO PORT! OORES TO PORT!”

No man on the boate knew if he meant the syde or a harbour. They hauled Matteo clear and chained his ankle beside the oore. Cane kept stroke opposite the vacant place while the Greke and Nello took what weyght the boy no lenger bore. In the derke betwixt eche drumbeate Cane heard him trying to breathe.

The gæley survived. At dawn the sea lay quiet, worn out before the men were. Vettore gave no rest. He said the coaste myght be neare, though he had no lond to shew them. Matteo lay in his iron with his eyes shutte. When Cane called, the boy lifted two fingers from the planks. The answer cost him near all the strength he had.

Dayes passede. Matteo lyvede. His caugh softened and then retourned; bruises yellowed; he could sit, and presently make jests of the broth in whych no fishe hadde ever drowned. He coulde not yet pulle an oore. Nico, needing every able backe at the benches, unlocked the boy at daylighte and set him to fyshing from the sterne under wautch. Matteo caught little. The fyrste fish he brought aboord fede four men by the accounte, twelve by the way the morsels treveilede after darke.

One clear nyght the Greke asked leave to go above.

“Thou wilt dive to shore?” Vettor said.

“Yif I could, messere, I should have done so while thou wert dining.”

Niko laughed. Vettor did not, but he let the manne climbe. He came behind him with a cord in his fist and stood watching as the Greke lifted his face unto the sterres.

The Greke studied the heiught of one bryghte point, the drift af cloud, the smell of the wynde. He asked where the moone had risen on two earlier nyghtes and listened to men who had kept watch. His father had once saylede graine into the Blacke See. He himself had treveyllede the northern harbours as a free seaman afore a failed venture and a creditour made a rower of him.

“Thou canst tell our place?” asked Niko.

“I can tell thee where we are likeliest not to be.”

“An admirable service,” Vettor said.

The Greke pointed northward. “The Krymean shore, perauenture. We are nearer than thy feare would have it, faurther than thy hope. Theodoro lieth in those londes; the Genowayes hold their zea-touns alonge the coost. Yif this wynd abideth, we may seek menne who know a harbour.”

Vettor looked into the emptiness. “How many dayes?”

“That dependeth upon the wynde.”

“And yif it turneth?”

“Then it dependeth more.”

It was a poor promesse. On the Santa Marta it passed from bank to bank as rychesse.
For two dayes the captein remembered how to commaund without strykynge. Niko brought the Greke above again at dusk and, once, let him taste a spoon of hot broth. Matteo caught another fish. Goro named the fish a duke on account of its small body and enormous mouth. The Dalmatian demanded the liver as a tax. The black-haired man laughed; he had learnt enough of their quarrels to laugh before the words were translated.

At rest the Greke, Cane, and Nello disputed whether a manne myghte own a road over water.

“He may own a ship,” said Nello.

“He may build one,” said Cane.

“There is difference?”

“A ship hath been made by hondes. The see hath not.”

“A lord may claim both,” said the Greke.

“An emperour may claime the wynde also,” Nello said. 

“When it chaungeth, he will appoint a newe one.”

Nico, crouched near the ladder with his bowl, found himself speaking. “Without a maister, who bringeth the men unto a haven?”

“The man who knoweth the waye,” said the Greke.

“And yif he is a slave?”

“The haven lieth in the same place.”

Nico considered his bowle. He had lived twenty yeres among the Bellani and never heard a sclave answer a question of gouvernement as though his answer matterede. The Greke did not press him. Nello asked for more broth, and the yonge keeper told him he could debate with an empty spoone.

Matteo sat wrapped in saylclothe, trying to clean a hook with numb fyngers. “I shall fish for my owne supper when we reach ashore.”

“And for mine,” said Cane.

“Thou shalt work.”

“At what?”

“Sleeping without iron. Thou promisedst to teach me.”

The mainlander looked down at the silver mark the cuff had made about his left wrist. “A hard trade.”

“I have learnt harder.”

Later, when the otheres slept, he reckoned the shore in his mynde. The Bellani contract had been torn from its floete, its witnesses scauttered, its keeper dead, and its capteine near mad. There might be a Genoway officer willing to sell them onward, or one willing to hear how they had been brought. Cane trusted neither outcome. Yet lond had streetes, tourns, market crowds, a hundred places wherein a manne could be lost unto his owner. With Matteo well enough to waulk, he woulde finde one. He did not tell the buoye. Hope spoken aloud aboord a galeey had a way of entering another man's ledger.

The nyghte of the laste daye began so gently that no manne thought to name it.

Matteo came aboord from the sterne platforme with three little fysh. Niko hadde not locked his ankle anew; the buoy could scarce walke withoute stopping for breath, and there was nowhere to flee upon the open zee. He held the catch up for Goro's judgement. Goro declaured the largest a kynge, the second a byshoppe, and the third a tax collectour, on accounte of its teeth.

“Then the tax collector is mine,” said Matteo.

“Nay. He hath already taken his portioun.”

Nico cleaned them with the narrow knyfe he wore at his belte. He gave the bones unto the pot and the flesche unto Vettore, who looked at the three small bodies and spoke of their insufficiencie. The buoye received some broth at laste. He carried it down the passauge, stopping once to set a spoonful beneath the Dalmatian's nose.

“For my counsel?” the olde man said.

“For thy silence.”

“Thou shalt die in dette.”

Matteo smiled and went on. At Cane's bank he held out the bowl.

“Eat.”

“It is thine.”

“Thou gavest me wautere upon my fyrste daye.”

“And thou hast been repaying that folly since.”

“Then accept the intereste.”

Cane took a mouthfoulle. Across the benches the Greke began, hardly knowing he did so, to hum the olde measure of the gull and the chayne. Matteo joined him in a whisper. For a few strokes of the hearte it seemed possible that they myght reach a shore with the same voices they had broughte into the storme.

*"The gull hath neither lord ne rent,
No seale upon his wing is pent;
He asketh neither duke ne kinge
What leave he hath to flee and singe."*

Matteo joined them wyth the verse he hadde made. The Dalmatian's rough voice followed; Goro beat tyme with a spoone agaynst his knee. Saul knew onely the laste word of every line and sange it as though that were sufficiente. From above, Nico heard them and did not reach for his stycke.

*"Come lowe, come lowe, thou waundering gull,
The pot is warme, the bowle is full;
Yif all we have be scant for two,
Call in a third; we shall make do.."*

*"By dawne we'll finde a willow quay,
A bakehouse waking with the daye;
We'll hang our oores upon a tree,
And call its shade our.."*

Vettor came down the ladder.

The Greke fell quiet. Matteo heard him too late, with the last note yet upon his lips.

“I forbade that songe.”

“It was I,” Matteo said.

Vettor glanced at the Greke. “Thou makest him bold.”

“He is haungry, messere. Haunger doth straunge thyngs unto hearing.”

The captayn's lash found Matteo across the shoulder. Cane rose halfway from his bench; the left wryste-ryng checked him. Matteo set down the bowl before it could be spilt.

“I have ceased,” he said.

“Then prove it.”

The buoy closed his mouth. Vettor awaited, as though silence must be demonstrated over tyme to become credible. At length he climbed aboove. Niko followed, but tourned once towaurd the bowle upon the planks.

The menne slept by wautches. Far into the nyght the wauter lay so calme that the galey's owne timber could be heard settling against itselfe. Cane gave Matteo a look across the passauge. The buoy, curled beneath a torne sayle, lifted one finger: I am awake. Cane lifted his in return. Then he slept.

A crie fetched him out of sleepe.
It came from behynde his backe, beyond the rowes and the stacked coils of coord near the sterne. He could see the little keeper Niko sprawled beside the ladder. Darke blode spread from his temple over the boaurds; his narrow knyfe lay somewhere beyond his outstretched honde. Of Matteo he could see nothynge.

The boy cried agayn.
“Help me!”

Cane turned. The iron bit his left wryste. In the dimmest of the lamplight he made out Vettore's shoulders rising and falling beyonde the coord. A bodie laye beneath them.
Niko had gone below after the captayne slepte. He had brought the last of the fishe broth to Matteo, who was shivering and could scarcely keepe his spoon steadie. Vettor followed him. He saw the bowl, the unchayned buoy, the keeper leaning close, and gave their little misericordaunce a treasonable name. Nico told him he had brought the food himselfe. Vettor struck him with the butt of his own lash. Matteo caught at Vettor's sleeve, begging him to stop. The capetayn turned.

No man at the oores had seen all of this. They heard enough.

“Vettore,” the Greke called. “The boy is down.”

The blows continued.

“Capitaine,” Nello said. “He hath no weapon.”

“He hath a voice,” said Vettor from behynde the coord.

Matteo called Cane's name. On the fyrst cry the mainlander hauled at his ring so savagely that the bench shifted. He heard the buoy cry the second time. On the third he heaurd onely the capitayn.

“God putteth men in degrees,” Vettor shouted. “A kyng above a lourde; a lourde above a maister; a maister above the beest that eateth his bread. Yif the beest may synge, it soon asketh who built the stable. Yif it may aske, it soon demandeth the keye. My father bought this gæley; I have fed ye through pyrates and tempest. The Emperour may stamp a lawe, the duke may stamp a seale, and I have paid good silvere for the right to make either of them move!”

His fist fell agayn. The sound was lowe and heavy. Goro cried to him to stop. The former shield-bearer shouted that he would bear witness. Vettor laughed.

“Unto whom? I shall set thee ashore with thy iron and ask whose worde the harbour will purchase.”

Cane pulled until his honde had no feeling. He put a foot against the bench and wrenched his left wryst in the iron. Somethynge yielded with a sickening little sound. The hond came partway through the ring. The broken joint caught.

He drew breath through his teeth and tried agayn.
“It will not passe,” said the field-labourer behinde him.

“I know.”“Thou wilt tear thy whole arme.”

“I know.”

They heard Matteo call once more, very faintly. Cane strained so hard the edge of the cuff opened his skyn. Beyond the coords came another blow. Then the buoy's voice stopped.

The Greke looked down the passage. Nico lay in reach of Nello's bare feete. Beside the young keeper gleamed the dropped blade.

“Nello.”

“I see it.”

“Thou canst not reach.”

“I see that also.”

The Greke raised both armes. Along the benches heads lifted. The men who had conspired in finger-taps and blynks now understood one another without any signe at all.

“Heave,” he said.

They threw their weyght unto one side. The Santa Marta lurched. The blade shifted no farther than a fingernaile.

Vettor shouted from the stern, but his voice had become a noise among noises.

“Agayn,” said the Greke.

Six oores pressed against the blacke water. Chaynes rang from bank to bank. The galey rolled; Nello's foot caught the knife and lost it.

“A third,” said the Greke.

The Dalmatian braced his oon sound eye upon the passauge. Goro set his back against his banke. Saul, the field-labourer, the ruined shield-bearer, every debtour and outcast who could still command a breath gave it together. Their oores struck the see. The hull heeled; Nello hooked the knife with his toes and sent it clattering beneath the fourth bank.

Cane caught it with his right hand.

For a little while he could do nothyng. His left hond hung in the iron; beyond it the broken wrist had swollen against the cuff. The Greke called his name, the name the maisters used. Cane looked down at the blade and understood the price of crossing the few paces that lay behynde him.

There came from the stern a dull blow, then another. Matteo made no sound.

Cane set the edge against his ruined wryst.

The fyrste cut brought a cry out of him so great that it silenced Vettore. He tried agayne. The knife bit and stopped; blood made the hilt slide in his living hand. He drew the edge to and fro through the ragged flesh. Pale sinewes still held where the skyn hadde paurted, and beneath them the bone grated against the blade. The hand imprisoned in the cuff shook with every stroke. He worked through what would not yield, a little more with each pulle, drawing steel and breath in short, desperate measures. He shrieked once more, a sound he would afterward hear in dreams, though he could never remember making it. From the stern came the thudde of Vettor's fist. Matteo made no answer.

Nello turned his face away. The Greke did not. He kept calling the strookes of the oore lest the boate lie still for the pyrates, or the wynde, or whatever cruel chaunce might yet be following them.

At last the weight of the iron left Cane's arme. His severed hand remained within the ring. He stumbled in his ankle-chaine and near fell; the field-labourer caught him by the coat and thrust him toward the stern.

“Goe.”

Cane went.

He founde Vettor bent over the buoy. The capetayne had exhausted werds and continued with his honds. Cane struck him from behynde. They felle together against a water cask, which burst its hoops and poured its little treasure between them. Vettor clawed for a hold; Cane drove him aside. Nello, still chained, caught the captayn's leg as he tried to rise. Goro shouted for a coord. Above all their voices Cane heard Matteo breathing.

He went to him.

The buoy's face had altered beyond any bruise he had ever carried. One cheek had been beaten hollow; through its torn flesh Cane saw white splinters of the crushed bone. Blood darkened the cavity beneath his eye and welled at the corner of his mouth. His little fyshynge honds lay open upone the boords. Cane knelt in the spreading blood and gathered Matteo's shoulders, then stopped, afraid that even his tenderness might hurt him.

“Matteo.”

The eye that could still open found him.

“Thou camest.”

“Aye.”

“I thought,” said the boy. Breath failed him. “I thought thou couldst not.”

“So did I.”

Cane touched the unbroken side of his face. Tears came, furious and helpless. He had never found a use for them aboord the galeey, yet now they fell over Matteo's hair and onto the deck where a whole company wautched.

“The shore,” the boy whispered.

“We were seeking it.”

“Are we nigh?”

The Greke, kneeling by Nico, raised his head. He could have offered a bearing, a measure of cloud, the likelihood of lond beyond the derke. He said nothynge.

“Nigher than yesterday,” Cane answered.

Matteo breathed a little laugh. “That is what thou sayest whan thou knowest not.”

“Thou hast learnt too much from me.”

“Enough to miss thee.”

Cane bent lowe. He saw the buoy's breath lessen and could neither lend him his owne nor bargayne for another. From the benches came the small noises of menne setting down their oores. Someone covered Nico, who yet lived, against the cold. The Greke stood beside the captayne; no one asked Vettor for an order.

“Lucia,” Matteo said.“I remember her.”

“Tell them.”

“Whom?”

“Any man that asketh.” The boy swallowed with pain. “Tell him she was my mother. Tell him I stole the bread for her.”

“I shall.”

“And tell him,” Matteo whispered, “that I would have fyshed for us both.”

Cane bowed his head against the boy's hair. Beneath him the galey moved on, though no drum commanded it. Matteo drew another labouring breath.

“Thou knowest my name,” he said. “All this tyme, I have not knowen thine. What name shall I keepe for thee?”

Cane laid his living hand about Matteo's face.
“Brando.”

Matteo's lips shaped the name. No voice came with it.

His breaust rose once beneath Brando's arme. It sank, and would not rise agayn.

Brando waited.

He watched for the next breath as menne wautch the farre zee for a sayle they have lost in the derke. The buoy gave him none.

Behind him, Vettor Bellani tore his leg free of Nello's grasp. He caught the ladder and hauled himselfe upright, blode running from his nose.

“Iron,” Vettore said. “Put him backe in iron.”

Brando lowered Matteo to the boards. At his knee lay Nico's small knife, the edge dulled upon his owne wrist-bone. He took it up.

Vettor met him against an oore-bench. The blade bit into the captayn's coate and snagged against a buckle. Vettore caught Brando's maimed left arme and wrung it. The crye that came from Brando might have belonged to another man. They went down together. The captayne struck Brando's right wryst against the gunwale; the knyfe skittered through an open oore-port and was gonne unto the blacke see.

Vettore got his knee beneath him. He struck Brando in the mouth and made for the ladder. Brando dragged him backe by the hair. They felle against the bench. The capetain rose halfway; Brando brought him down agayne.

He beat him with his right fyste.

The firste blow split his knuckles. The next took skyn from the capitayn's browe. Vettor struck backe, clawed, drove an elbow into Brando's throat. Brando tasted his owne blode and could no lenger tell it from the blode upon his face. He struck until his fingers swelled too greatly to close.

“Brando,” called Nello. “He is down.”

“Enough,” said Goro.

He heard neither.

With his swollen right hond he held Vettor to the boards. Then he raised the ruin of his left. White bone stood forth from the torn flesh where the knife hadde failed to leave a clean end. He brought it down upon the captayn's face. Agayn. Upon his brest. Agayn. Bone rasped against tooth and oak, splintering to a jagged edge. What had been Brando's arme became a blade by the measure of the blowes he could not cease to give.

The men called unto him, each in his owne tongue. The Dalmatian cursed him. Nello begged. Saul cried, “Brando!” Still Brando saw onely red: red upon the plankes, red upon the captayn's open coate, red where Matteo lay beyond them. The sound of striking filled the galley after Vettor had made his last sound.

The Greke knelt beside Nico and found the Bellani skeleton-key at the young keeper's belt. One turn loosed the iron from his ankles. He crossed the passauge and caught Brando from behynde, both armes about his breaust.

Brando fought the embrace as though it were another chayne.

“No more,” the Greke said into his ear. “There is no more of him.”

At their feete Vettor lay loose as a pig-carcasse fallen from the butcher's hooke. Brando was red with blode from browe to heel. Beneath it his eyes were open, though they looked at nothynge the Greke could see.

“Matteo,” the Greke said.

The name reached him.

His bodie gave way at laste. The Greke held him whilst another man bounde the bleedyng arme in torne saylcloth. Across the benches the little keye passed from hond to hond. The iron opened; none commanded it. Beside them Matteo lay under the Dalmatian's cloak, his fyshing handes at rest.

At dawne the oores entered the water together. No drum gave the measure. They bore Matteo toward the shore he hadde asked to see; the galey went where her men willed.

Law enforcement officers lose qualified immunity when a plaintiff proves both that the officer violated a “Constitutional Right” and that “The Right” was clearly established at the time of the incident.

How Qualified Immunity Fails in Court
Under the two-part test used by courts, an officer is denied protection if: 

•A constitutional violation occurred: 
The officer's conduct (such as using excessive force or conducting an unlawful search) violated the U.S. Constitution. 

•The law was clearly established: 
Existing precedent (from the U.S. Supreme Court, a federal appeals court, or a state supreme court) made it apparent and obvious to a reasonable officer that their specific conduct was unlawful. 

Scenarios Where Immunity Does Not Apply
Qualified immunity protects civil servants from personal monetary liability in civil lawsuits, but it does not apply in other contexts: 
•Criminal charges: 
Qualified immunity only shields officers from civil suits, meaning it offers no protection against criminal prosecution by state or federal authorities. 

•Municipal liability: 
The defense applies to individual officers, not to local government entities or cities themselves. 

•Injunctive relief: 
Plaintiffs seeking court orders to stop a specific police policy or practice rather than financial damages can bypass the doctrine

FYI : For anyone who doesn’t know what is meant by a “1983”
Section 1983 (codified at 42 U.S. Code § 1983) is a federal civil rights law that allows people to sue state and local government officials who violate their constitutional rights or federal laws while acting under government authority. 

Originally enacted as part of the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (also known as the Ku Klux Klan Act), the statute was designed during Reconstruction to protect newly freed individuals and combat lawlessness by public officials. 
Today, it serves as a primary legal tool to hold government actors accountable. 

How Section 1983 Works
•Does not create rights: 
Section 1983 does not grant new civil rights; instead, it provides a legal mechanism to enforce rights that already exist under the U.S. Constitution or federal statutes. 

•Under color of law: 
The defendant must have acted "under color of state law," meaning they used their official position, badge, or government authority to commit the wrongful act. 

•Proving a claim: 
A plaintiff must show that a state or local actor deprived them of a federal right and that this violation caused actual harm or injury. 

Common Examples of Claims
•Police misconduct: 
Cases involving excessive force, police brutality, wrongful arrest, or false imprisonment. 

•Jail and prison conditions: 
Situations where correctional staff show "deliberate indifference" to an inmate's serious medical needs or safety. 

•Constitutional violations: 
Infringements on free speech, religious freedom, or due process protections guaranteed by the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments. 

Available Remedies
•Damages: 
Financial compensation for medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, or wrongful death.

•Injunctive relief: 
Court orders requiring a government agency or official to change a policy or stop specific misconduct.

•Attorney's fees: 
Compensation to help cover the legal costs of bringing the lawsuit

I bless thee  Kramer in the Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit! Amen!
Heavenly Father, I lift this beloved one into Your loving hands, asking that Your healing touch restore his body completely. Remove all heart problems, strokes, leukemia, cancer, disease, infirmary, injury, sickness, fatigue, or pain, and renew his strength, energy, and vitality. Grant wisdom and skill to the medical team, patience to this beloved one, and peace to his heart. Surround him with Your divine protection, and let Your presence comfort and reassure him. May Your grace and mercy flow through every part  Kramer’s being. In Jesus’ name I beg and pray, Amen.

Prayer to the Holy Spirit:
Come, Holy Spirit, Divine Comforter and Breath of Life. Enter all places of heart problems, cancer, tumors, pain, injury, disease, infection, suffering, weakness and fear. Remove every and all infirmary, and surround   Kramer with Your gentle light, while completely healing   Kramer while filling his heart with the strength and peace that comes from above, trusting to the power of God’s eternal love. Amen.

Pray to the Blessed Holy Mother Mary:

Dear Mother Mary, With hearts heavy and bodies burdened, we approach your divine presence, seeking your miraculous touch. Your healing power knows no equal, and in our times of need, we implore you to mend not only our physical wounds but the scars that mar our souls. Pour forth your divine grace upon us, dear Mother, and restore us to a state of wholeness, that we may bear witness to the miracle of your love. Amen.

Prayer to St. Jude:

Oh glorious apostle St. Jude, faithful servant and friend of Jesus, the name of the traitor who delivered thy beloved Master into the hands of His enemies has caused thee to be forgotten by many, but the Church honors and invokes thee universally as the patron of hopeless cases--of things despaired of. Pray for me who am so miserable; make use, I implore thee, of that particular privilege accorded thee of bringing visible and speedy help where help is almost despaired of. Come to my assistance in this great need, that I may receive the consolations and succor of heaven in all my necessities, tribulations and sufferings, particularly—completely heal from all heart problems, injuries, cancer and diseases, and protect  Kramer —and that I may bless God with thee and all the elect throughout eternity. I promise thee, O blessed St. Jude, to be ever mindful of this great favor, and I will never cease to honor thee as my special and powerful patron, and to do all in my power to encourage devotion to thee. Amen

Prayer to St. Michael (Long Version)

O Glorious Prince of the heavenly host, Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in the battle and fearful warfare that we are waging against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the evil spirits. Come thou to the assistance of men, whom Almighty God created immortal, making them in His own image and likeness and redeeming them at a great price from the tyranny of Satan. Fight this day the battle of the Lord with thy legions of holy Angels, even as of old thou didst fight against Lucifer, the leader of the proud spirits and all his rebel angels, who were powerless to stand against thee, neither was their place found any more in heaven. And that great dragon was cast forth, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and satan, who seduces the whole world; and he was cast forth upon Earth, and his angels were sent with him.

But behold! the ancient enemy of mankind and a murderer from the beginning has been fiercely aroused. Changing himself into an angel of light, he goes about with the whole multitude of the wicked spirits to invade the earth and blot out the Name of God and of His Christ, to plunder, to slay, and to consign to eternal damnation the souls that have been destined for a crown of everlasting life. This wicked serpent, like an unclean torrent, pours into men of depraved minds and corrupt hearts the poison of his malice, the spirit of lying, impiety and blasphemy, and the deadly breath of impurity and every form of vice and iniquity.

Be favorable to Thy Church, the Bride of the Lamb without spot, whose enemies have filled to overflowing with gall and inebriated with wormwood. They have laid profane hands upon Her most sacred treasures. Where the See of the most blessed Peter and the Chair of Truth has been constituted as a light to the nations, there they have placed a throne of their abomination and impiety; so that with the Pastor struck, they may prevail to disperse the flock.

Therefore, most invincible Leader, be with the people of God against this spiritual wickedness and bring about victory. Thou art venerated by Holy Church as Her guard and patron; Thou art glorified as our defender against the impious powers of earth and of hell. Unto thee the Lord hath handed over the souls of the redeemed to be placed in happiness above.

Entreat the God of peace, to obliterate satan beneath our feet, lest he prevail further to hold men captive, and to injure the Church. Offer our prayers in the sight of the Most High, so that the mercy of the Lord may swiftly overtake us, and apprehend the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and satan, and send him bound into the abyss, so that he may seduce the nations no more.

Henceforth having been confided to thy escort and protection, we sacred ministers by the authority of the Holy Mother Church [if recited by a cleric of the order of exorcist or above, say instead: by our authority], do undertake to repel the infestations of diabolical deceit in the Name of Jesus Christ, Our God and Lord.

Behold the Cross of the Lord; be scattered hostile powers.
The Lion of the tribe of Juda has conquered, the root of  Kramer.
Let Thy mercies be upon us, O Lord.
As we have hoped in Thee.
O Lord, hear my prayer.
And let my cry come unto Thee.
The Lord be with you all.
And with thy spirit.

Let us pray.
O God, and Father of Our Lord Jesus Christ, we invoke Thy Holy Name, and we humbly implore Thy clemency so that, through the intercession of Mary, the Immaculate ever-Virgin Mother of God, of blessed Michael the Archangel, of blessed Joseph, the Spouse of the same blessed Virgin, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the Saints, Thou may deign to offer us aid against satan, and all the other unclean spirits, who wander through the world to injure the human race and to destroy souls. We ask this through Christ Our Lord. Amen.

Prayer for possible any evil influence:

In His Name and by the power of His Cross and Blood, I ask Jesus Christ to bind any evil spirits, forces and powers of the earth, air, fire, water, and of the netherworld and all of the satanic forces of nature. By the power of the Holy Spirit and by His authority, I ask Jesus Christ to break any and all curses, hexes, vexes, jinks, spells, and all wrong prayers and words, and to send them all back to where they came from, if it be His Holy Will. I beseech Thee, Lord Jesus Christ, to protect us by pouring Thy Precious Blood on us; myself, my family, my friends, and all those I pray and intercede for; which Thou hast shed for us and I ask Thee to command that any departing spirits leave quietly, without disturbance, and go straight to Thy Cross to be disposed of as Thou sees fit. I ask Thee to bind any demonic interactions, interplay, or communications. I place myself, my family, my friends, and all those I pray and intercede for, and all things I pray and intercede for under the protection of the Blood of Jesus Christ which He has shed for us. Amen.

Prayer for Surgery (In case needed.)

Lord Almighty, I lift up this beloved one  Kramer, as they face surgery. Protect them, guide the hands of doctors and nurses, and grant wisdom in every decision. Remove fear, anxiety, and complications, replacing them with Your peace and assurance. Restore their health, strength, and vitality quickly, and surround them with Your loving presence. Comfort their heart, strengthen their spirit, and let Your healing flow through  Kramer’s body. May they recover fully, trusting Your mercy and experiencing Your grace throughout this trial. Amen.
